idiom_name: static inline wrapper function in a header
implementation_notes: C has no message send and no delegation mechanism, so the one-line method becomes an ordinary function: define it static inline next to the struct it serves, in the header, so every translation unit that calls it sees the body and the compiler can substitute the call. The C99 inline form without static has different linkage semantics - it is only a definition for inlining and the program must contain exactly one external definition - so static inline is the form that is safe in a header. What replaces the classic structure is nothing: there is no library or syntax that generates the wrapper, and a function-like macro, the only zero-call alternative, double-evaluates its arguments, cannot be stepped through in a debugger and has no address, so treat macros as a last resort.
pitfalls: A non-static inline definition in a header is not a definition for linkage purposes: without one translation unit providing the external definition (or making it static inline) the program is ill-formed or fails to link.
A macro twin of the wrapper evaluates its arguments more than once and disappears from stack traces; keep the wrapper a real function.
C has no namespaces or overloading, so two modules that both name a wrapper after the operation collide at link time - prefix the selector-like name with the module.
